content: It is essential to consider and discuss various approaches to palliative care within the national context. Some of these approaches can complement each other and may be implemented simultaneously, depending on the available resources and specific circumstances. This manual does not aim to provide clinical guidance for treating patients requiring palliative care. Instead, separate WHO guidelines on pain management and the management of common palliative care symptoms should be consulted for such purposes. The right to health is enshrined in numerous international and regional human rights treaties, such as Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights and Article 24 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Notably, the latter treaty has been ratified by every country except Somalia and the United States. Palliative care is often misunderstood as merely the administration of pain-relieving medications. While pain relief and the management of distressing symptoms are central to palliative care, its scope extends further. It aims to improve the quality of life and may even positively influence the course of illness. Palliative care affirms life and regards dying as a natural process. It integrates physical, psychological, social, cultural, and spiritual aspects of care. Patients are supported to live as actively as possible until death, and families are provided with assistance to cope during the patient’s illness and through bereavement. Palliative care neither hastens nor postpones death. Instead, it adheres to ethical principles, shared decision-making, and advanced care planning to identify patients’ priorities and goals for end-of-life care. A multidisciplinary team approach is employed, involving various healthcare and social care providers, as well as volunteers. Importantly, palliative care is not limited to hospitals; it can be delivered in any healthcare setting, including patients’ homes, and can be effectively implemented even in resource-limited environments. At a minimum, palliative care services should: Identify patients who could benefit from palliative care. Assess and reassess patients for physical, emotional, social, and spiritual distress, as well as evaluate family members for similar needs. Provide relief from pain and other distressing physical symptoms. Address spiritual, psychological, and social needs. Clarify patients’ values and establish culturally appropriate care goals. Primary palliative care practices can be categorized into four domains: physical care, psychological/emotional/spiritual care, care planning and coordination, and communication. Essential Practices in Primary Palliative Care: 1. Physical Care Needs: Address pain (all types), respiratory problems (e.g., dyspnea, cough), gastrointestinal issues (e.g., constipation, nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, mucositis, diarrhea), delirium, wounds, ulcers, skin lesions, insomnia, fatigue, anorexia, anemia, drowsiness, sedation, and sweating. 2. Psychological/Emotional/Spiritual Care Needs: Manage psychological distress, anxiety, depression, and suffering of family or caregivers. Address spiritual needs and existential distress. Provide bereavement support for families and caregivers. 3. Care Planning and Coordination: Identify available support and resources. Develop and implement care plans tailored to patients’ needs. Ensure access to essential medications, particularly opioids. Address the psychosocial and spiritual needs of care providers, including self-care. 4. Communication: Communicate effectively with patients, families, and caregivers about diagnosis, prognosis, treatment, symptoms, and end-of-life care. Set priorities collaboratively with patients and families. Provide clear information and guidance tailored to available resources. Identifying Patients Who Can Benefit from Palliative Care: Most patients with chronic, complex, or life-limiting health conditions, as well as those nearing the end of life, require palliative care. Early initiation of palliative care is crucial when a health problem becomes serious, complex, or life-threatening, even as disease-modifying treatments continue. Early identification of palliative care needs should be integrated into all healthcare settings. Assessing Patients’ and Families’ Needs: Palliative care begins with a comprehensive assessment of physical, emotional, social, spiritual, and cultural needs, as well as the values and preferences of patients and families. Validated tools, such as the Edmonton Symptom Assessment Scale (ESAS) and the Palliative Outcome Score (POS), can aid in this process. Patients and caregivers often require assistance with care organization and communication. Determining patients’ values and priorities is essential for creating an optimal care plan. Advance directives, such as living wills or powers of attorney, may be helpful, though some patients prefer family members to make decisions on their behalf. Relief of Pain and Other Symptoms: Pain is one of the most common and severe symptoms experienced by patients requiring palliative care. For example, 80% of patients with AIDS or cancer and 67% of those with cardiovascular disease or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease experience moderate to severe pain at the end of life. Pain is multidimensional, encompassing physical, emotional, psychosocial, and spiritual aspects. Effective symptom management requires treating underlying causes, using pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, and tailoring care to patients’ values and needs. Addressing Psychosocial and Spiritual Needs: Psychosocial care involves addressing the psychological, emotional, social, and financial well-being of patients and families. Psychological symptoms such as anxiety, depression, and delirium should be assessed and treated with the same rigor as physical symptoms. Social suffering may arise from poverty, stigma, or discrimination, and palliative care workers can provide resources to alleviate these challenges. Spiritual distress and existential concerns should be treated with equal priority, potentially involving spiritual care providers or therapies such as dignity-centered care, mindfulness, or art therapy. Supporting Families and Caregivers: Family caregivers play a vital role in palliative care, particularly for patients who wish to die at home. Caregivers often face physical and psychological challenges, financial strain, and social isolation. Their needs should be assessed, and appropriate support provided. Caregivers may benefit from information about their role, symptom management for the patient, and respect for the patient’s values. While caregiving can be demanding, it also has the potential for positive outcomes with adequate support.
